source: វិធានការចម្រុះគ្រប់គ្រងដំណាំ លើដំណាំស្រូវ (Integrated Pest Management on Rice), training slide deck, Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries of Battambang province, presented by Ms. Yem Sophy, Oct 20, 2017 (contact: ysophy168@gmail.com, 012 558 312)
text: Rice gall midge (Orseolia oryzae) resembles a small mosquito; the adult female has an orange/reddish abdomen and the male a darker abdomen. Eggs are laid singly or in small groups on young rice leaves near the growing point; the hatching larva burrows into the tiller's growing point, causing it to form a hollow, tube-like gall ('silver shoot') instead of a normal leaf, and that tiller never produces a panicle. Outbreaks build up especially fast where continuous rice cropping with overlapping planting dates gives the short-lived adult midge a constant supply of young, susceptible tillers nearby; a female can lay over 100 eggs. [The deck states the egg-to-next-generation cycle takes roughly 4-5 days; as with other short life-cycle figures in this source, this should be checked against a primary reference.] Recorded natural enemies include Platygasterid, Eupelmid, and Pteromalid parasitic wasps attacking the larva inside the gall, and a predatory phytoseiid mite feeding on gall-midge eggs.
